A self is a forest. A self is a ship. A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

Kahlil Gibran (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life, takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic The Madman (public library | free ebook).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated the Japanese concept of ma.)

In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:

First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years, with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.

Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary existence.

Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self who would rebel against this madman.

Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell, who would protest against serving this madman.

Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self, the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is I, not you, who would rebel.

Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who, with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.

Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?

When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy submission.

But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness, which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself, then revisit Hermann Hesse on discovering the soul beneath the self.

#9301. 5 Things We’re Saying No to This Holiday Season

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Before you say yes this holiday season, ask yourself what you’re saying yes to. Consider the feelings that come up for you when you think about it. Is it excitement about seeing the people you love? Is it dread at the anticipation of planning, conflict, or grief? For some, it’s all of the above.

Recent polls find that nearly 9 in 10 (89%) U.S. adults report holiday stressors (APA, 2023). Tensions arise due to finances, family conflict, grief, and other factors. Stress takes away from the pleasurable aspects of the season, which should include reconnection and rest.

Sometimes that is easier said than done. Here are 5 things we're saying no to this holiday season and strategies to achieve the happy holidays we deserve.

Sometimes that family holiday announcement sounds like a demand rather than an invitation. “Dinner is at 4 pm sharp. See you there!” Everyone assumes you’ll be there, and no one asks questions. They don’t ask if you can take time off work, afford the trip, or have other plans. You feel obligated to attend despite any barriers you are facing.

Almost no one will tell you that you are allowed to consider your own needs before you RSVP yes. Ask yourself whether you have the time, energy, and money to participate this year. If the answer is no, it’s alright. Your family may be disappointed, and you may feel a little guilty, but it’s worth asking which will weigh on you more: the guilt of saying no or the cost of saying yes.

In toxic families, it’s the once-over as soon as you enter the room. Before you’ve even had a chance to sit down, someone has made a joke about your weight or graying hair, offered a backhanded compliment about the dish you contributed, or slipped in a dig about your personal life.

You may feel hurt, sad, or even angry, and you don’t have to ignore those feelings to preserve the holiday spirit. You can be silent and stone-faced to let the “joke” fall flat. You might excuse yourself and regroup in another room. If you want to address it directly and call out the hidden meaning, you can say, “That felt like a dig,” or ask, “What do you mean by that?” What you don’t have to do is tolerate disrespect.

When you want everyone to feel loved, it’s easy to slip into spending more than you intended. If you’ve ever hosted a large family gathering, you know how quickly the groceries and gifts add up. And if you’re the one who hosts every year, it can feel like the work and the bill are yours by default.

Before you do anything, set a budget. Then share the work in ways that play into everyone’s strengths. Maybe enlist the nephew who can roast meat or the cousin who loves to bake, and assign cleanup to the one you prefer to stay out of the kitchen. Suggest rotating hosting duties. Do a gift exchange rather than buying individual gifts for everyone. You can show your love to your family with limits.

In some families, playing the dutiful daughter (or son) means everyone assumes you’ll make the holidays happen. Often it’s the family matriarch or the eldest daughter who initiates the first call about the holiday plans and is the one still in the kitchen long after everyone else has gone home. She is the family “glue” who keeps track of the invites, remembers who can’t eat what, and figures out where to seat the relatives who aren’t speaking. By the time the holiday arrives, she’s too tired to enjoy the fruits of her labor.

If that sounds like you, name it. People who have never hosted may not realize all of the hidden effort that goes into an event. Bring it to their attention. Set limits on what you will do and ask for help, but don’t micromanage. If the person assigned to bring the rolls forgets, skip the rolls this year. If no one steps up, step back anyway. Plan a smaller, more intimate gathering that won’t leave you frazzled at the end of it.

The holidays aren’t the same after you’ve lost a loved one, and the first holiday season after a loss can be especially difficult. Family traditions may be upended. The person who always hosted and made everyone’s favorite dish is gone. Tensions that surface after the loss may still be hanging in the air.

Take a moment to evaluate your feelings. Ask yourself what you feel up to this year. Maybe it’s not the year to take on hosting duties, or perhaps you stop by for dessert rather than staying the entire day. You can choose to honor your loved one by retaining old traditions or step into the next chapter with new traditions in their memory. You can miss someone deeply and still make room for moments of joy this holiday season.

It might seem strange that saying no could be the start of a happy holiday. The beauty is that you get to decide what a happy holiday looks like for you, and that it can change from year to year. Ask yourself what would make the holidays feel good to you this year and do it.

American Psychological Association. (2023). Even a joyous holiday season can cause stress for most Americans. https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2023/11/holiday-season-stress

#9300. Russian strikes damage historic buildings in Kyiv and Odesa, including World Heritage sites

St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv Photo by Wavemeart, via Wikimedia Commons

Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.

At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.

“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.

The neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.

The Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.

A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.

Berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”

The minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to plan for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.

Unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.

The strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin said this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.

A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was launched last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.

The bombing of several buildings including in the historic city centre—a World Heritage Site—has been strongly condemned by Unesco

The 11th-century World Heritage Site was damaged by a strike on Tuesday

A monastery in Kyiv was set ablaze by a missile strike in the latest offensive against the country, with residential buildings also targeted

The UN body is monitoring heritage sites by satellite and plans a meeting with Ukrainian museum directors to safeguard collections

#9299. 3 Things to Do When Your Adult Child Pulls Away

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Just last week, my parent coaching client looked at me quizzically while describing a recent text from her son. The text was just a photo of her son's dog wearing (or at least trying to wear) a cap of a major league baseball team. She said, "Dr. Jeff, it's been two months since I last heard from him, and of course, I immediately smiled when I saw the pic."

This hurt, Mom soon added, "But I had no idea what to do next." This client elaborated that her fingers led her to compose and immediately delete five responses prior to sending them. She added, "No matter what I do, he will pull away again, anyway."

The client above was struggling with how to respond after a long lag in communication with her adult child. She didn't know whether to joke about the cute picture, or tell her son she missed him, or ask further about Thanksgiving. For any parents in similar situations, it can be maddening to feel unsure about how to respond.

And, if you have not spoken to your adult child for over six months or even years, the absence of that relationship has a huge, seemingly constant presence. By this I mean that often in these partial or full-on estrangement situations, the reality is that minimal or no contact does not take away from the internal emotional upheaval that comes from the desire to reconnect.

It is easy to feel helpless in the face of not seeing your adult child or not having the level of connection that you value. In my parent coaching work, I encourage parents to focus on three things they can do no matter how long it's been since they last heard their grown child's voice.

Finish this sentence: "What I miss most about my grown child today is__________." Some parents might reply that they wish they knew how their son was doing. Maybe, as in the early example of the dog photo, a parent misses lighter moments of laughter. Maybe a song reminds you of your adult child.

Identifying what you miss is tangible and healthy because it helps you process difficult feelings like sadness, disappointment, nostalgia, or loneliness. For example, that treasured memory of you and your daughter going for a ride and belting out a shared favorite song may weigh heavily on your mind. Consider sharing these thoughts with trusted relatives, friends, a therapist, or a parent coach. Sometimes it helps to have someone just say, "Tell me more."

Some parents have been deeply hurt by how their adult child has treated them, and yes, sometimes the reasons for the distance are unclear, and this can feel maddening. At the same time, if you genuinely regret anything you said or did, you can be specific about what you're apologizing for while still honoring your own experience of what happened.

Consider your adult daughter saying to you, "When I tell you what bothered me that you did when I was growing up, you kept twisting it to make it my fault and giving me advice." You may remember trying to help. But hold on, because, at the same time, maybe you can recall trying to give her advice when she said, "Dad, can I finish my point?"

Looking at your own behaviors in this way gives you an honest point of reflection to start. You could then say, "I've been reflecting on times I rushed in to give you advice, and it got in the way of better understanding what you were going through, and I'm sorry." This type of dialogue not only shows that you are taking responsibility, but you are also modeling self-awareness to your adult child.

In my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!, I explore how easily a parent's regret can turn into a feeling of indebtedness. In the parent coaching trenches, I have seen how tempting it is for parents to promise their adult children something to bring them closer. Please keep in mind that you can offer a sincere apology and still take your time to decide what you can reasonably do or give. For parents who are totally out of contact, I suggest you write down what you regret and keep it private.

This third point is really hard for parents missing their adult children. If several messages go unanswered, give your adult child room to reach out. If they asked for no contact, honor that request. Believe it or not, adult children in these situations often share with me that they still love and even miss their parents, even when they outwardly state they want no contact. Just remember what I wrote above: The absence of contact still has a great presence in both your mind and that of your adult child.

Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted.

What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound.

As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life, “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.”

Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love.

There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son:

Silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full.

When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us.

The silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve.

A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself. Pärt puts it more gently:

One does not have to speak. But one must love. One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book. But one must love… If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love.

I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago:

Silence with you is like the faint delicious Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed: Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming, The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest. Silence with you is like a kind departure From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd Into a wide and greenly barren meadow, Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud; Or like one held upon the sands at evening, When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed Sails that move darkly on the edge of night.

#9297. The Courage to Question Our Own Certainty

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

There are a plethora of potentially polarizing issues these days in all aspects of our lives! It seems that we can hardly get a point of view on the table before a fellow conversationalist debunks our idea and discredits us along the way. Take your pick from a bushel full of igniting issues, whether it be global warming, wars, increasing the tax percentage for the very wealthy, or the strengths and weaknesses of our favorite political personalities; there will be no shortage of strong opinions. You can also be assured that before the full set of points of view are exposed or explored, one or more folks will have already decided what the correct point of view should be.

Our positioning and decisions on an issue seem like they happen in the blink of an eye. This instant judgement can create ill will, stress for us and the other, and can challenge or ruin long-standing relationships. Furthermore, it will likely lead to a suboptimal exploration and resolution of the salient points of view. The pivot that I would like to explore is realizing that although our interpretations and positions usually feel quite certain to us, they most likely do not represent the whole of the reality of that situation; they are a narrower, biased slice of the problem or solution.

I would like to explore what can happen when we can loosen our grip on our story/point of view, and instead consider what might ensue if we instead question our own certainty. This, of course, would require slowing down enough to really listen first and then explore the fuller reality of the situation together; then, with skillful listening and openness to other ways of thinking, we can have a meaningful and civil dialogue.

We seem to be experiencing a plethora of fractured conversations, competing accounts of the truth, information overload, and fear about the future, all of which are leading to what we might call “contemporary exhaustion.” And if the impact of this on us personally wasn’t enough, the relational tension as well as the societal and political challenges are at an all-time high. It is so much more likely that answers to our difficult questions will land somewhere in the middle of the two opposing extremes being debated, or in a yet-to-be-discovered “third alternative” idea that cannot possibly be uncovered because of the anger, tension, and lack of listening in the interchange. Just to ground this idea in one statistic: the American Psychological Association's Stress in America survey, "A Crisis of Connection," reported that 62% of adults considered societal divisions a significant stressor in their lives.

If you are willing to have the “courage to suspend the certainty” of your initial interpretation and allow for more information, thoughts, and feelings to emerge between you and another, amazing things can happen. Try following a simple practice of what I will call “thoughtful receptivity” using these 4 steps. Imagine that, before you know it, you are in a polarizing conversation with challenging points of view and heated feelings emerging. Each side draws his/her sword, and the point-counterpoint debate begins. You have enough presence to realize you are in the battle, and it likely will not end well. You feel triggered and notice the same for the other person. You remember this practice and do the following:

We all have the tendency to confuse the story we have crafted and are trying to tell with the whole truth about a situation. Perhaps a better way to proceed is to remain open to what we have not yet explored or understood, remain open to another way of thinking about a situation, and remain open to the other person. If we could find the grace to do so, we might learn to see and understand more deeply before we judge. All of this ultimately requires that we develop the courage to question our own certainty. If we could do so, it is very likely that our world would become a much better, kinder place to live and thrive.

American Psychological Association. (2025). Stress in America 2025: A crisis of connection. https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/stress-in-america/2025

#9296. Should Scientists Ignore Philosophers of Science?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

The eminent evolutionary biologist and modeller John Maynard Smith was once asked about Karl Popper and the philosophy of science. His answer was not flattering. His impression was that scientists who take the philosophy of science seriously, and allow their research to be influenced by philosophical preconceptions, are "far more likely to do themselves harm than good". He loved reading philosophy of science and was always ready to argue about it, he added, but he did not believe that one should allow oneself to be influenced by it when actually thinking about science.

This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic. These are quite radical words, and though Maynard Smith's generalisation is untenable, there is an important insight to be extracted.

If modellers approach the philosophical literature on models with the goal of figuring out what models are and what a good model is, they might easily find themselves lured into naive monistic views of models that fail to represent the full epistemic richness of modelling practices, thereby turning them into worse scientists than they could have otherwise been.

This could happen in several ways. For instance, models with epistemic functions not recognised by narrow monist accounts might be discarded. Consider, for example, models with weak predictive power, but great generality and insight into complex systems.

Perhaps Maynard Smith's worry is most strongly illustrated in economics, where Milton Friedman and Karl Popper are taken to have the "last word" in any methodological debate, and are frequently invoked to both defend and criticise the work of modellers. They are perhaps paradigm cases of monist thinking. Friedman argued that the only relevant desideratum in science concerns predictive power, while Popper argued that what matters is falsifiability.

These accounts of science have received extensive criticism over the last decades. Indeed, the philosopher Alex Rosenberg argued that Friedman's naive picture single-handedly justified the existence of philosophy of economics as a distinct profession. Economists, however, are unlikely to read much if any work on methodology beyond Friedman and Popper. As the economist Dani Rodrik notes, economic methodology is relegated to specialised journals and, more importantly, is not really being taught in graduate school.

The result is that economists seem to believe that their science operates according to a simple form of falsificationism, a picture of science that, most contemporary philosophers of science would agree, both misrepresents scientific practice and provides the wrong ideal of how science ought to function.

The obvious counter to Maynard Smith's concern is that it is not an argument against the philosophy of science, but rather against bad philosophy of science, which limits, rather than fosters, insights into the richness of the epistemic tools available to scientists.

Philosophers are not innocent here. Some debates in the philosophy of science rest on such monist motivations to seek univocal accounts of laws, explanation, species, functions, preferences, and many more. As Peter Godfrey-Smith emphasised, one of the hazards of philosophy is the temptation to come up with theories that are "too broad and sweeping". This hazard has not been avoided in the philosophical literature on models. Many philosophers of science seem to be under the impression that once we figure out what "models" are and how they work, we can finally get a handle on all the other pressing questions in the philosophy of science. I argue that this way of thinking about models is grounded in a mistake.

A philosophy of science worth reading takes the plurality, diversity, and richness of models and modelling practices seriously. It does not hand scientists a single criterion for good science.

Economists, Rodrik argues, need a better story about the kind of science they practise, and some economists have recently engaged with philosophical questions themselves, seeking contact with philosophers of economics in the process. Philosophers of science, in turn, should turn more of their attention toward both the social sciences and the philosophy of the social sciences. Their lack of engagement with this rich literature is a historical omission that may have provided a misguided understanding of how science works.

Should scientists ignore philosophers? They should ignore those who tell them that there is only one way of doing science well.

Veit, W. (2019). Model Pluralism. Philosophy of the Social Sciences, 50(2), 91–114. https://doi.org/10.1177/0048393119894897 [Download]

Friedman, M. (1953). The Methodology of Positive Economics. In Essays in Positive Economics, 3–43. University of Chicago Press.

Godfrey-Smith, P. (2003). Theory and Reality: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science. University of Chicago Press.

Maynard Smith, J. (1997). Interview by Richard Dawkins. Web of Stories. https://www.webofstories.com/play/john.maynard.smith/99

Popper, K. (1959). The Logic of Scientific Discovery. Routledge.

Rodrik, D. (2015). Economics Rules: Why Economics Works, When It Fails, and How to Tell the Difference. Oxford University Press.

Rosenberg, A. (2009). If Economics Is a Science, What Kind of a Science Is It? In H. Kincaid and D. Ross (eds), The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Economics, 55–67. Oxford University Press.

#9295. First Frieze Abu Dhabi proves successful for the region's dealers, despite geopolitical jitters

The inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) opened to a promising start. Strong sales were reported across many galleries, and the fair had an energy that spread from the stands to the garden outside at the Manarat Al Saadiyat, where guests lingered for hours over the unlikely combination of pizza and champagne.

“They’re looking after us very well here,” one established Dubai collector said. “Unlike at other fairs, where we feel pressured to buy, here we can take a breather and reflect on things. The art world is very collegiate in this region and the collectors are here to support.”

Like its name, Frieze Abu Dhabi was a mix of two halves. The successor to the long-standing Abu Dhabi Art fair that has been operating, under various names, in the UAE capital since 2007, the fair is co-run by Frieze Fairs and the UAE government’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT). Accordingly, the event blended elements of Abu Dhabi Art’s programme with those more familiar to Frieze's flagship event in Regent’s Park.

Chief among these is the Ladies’ Day—the day before the public opening that is reserved for Abu Dhabi’s sheikhas—and the pre-bound book of available works that is sent around to the city’s royals.

Meanwhile Frieze brought its art fair expertise, giving the fair a better layout and an improved allover experience. “The fair still has its Abu Dhabi Art soul but feels a lot tighter in terms of the number of galleries and the selection,” said Taymour Grahne, whose eponymous gallery moved from New York to London and has now settled in Dubai. Grahne was showing a series of mosaics by the Palestinian artist Ala Younis, which by the opening day had mostly sold.

Most of the galleries’ presentations were rooted in the Wanasa (West Asia, North Africa and South Asia) region. Standout booths included that of the Cairo gallery Art Talks/Kanafani's solo presentation of the Egyptian surrealist Samir Rafi, and the Dubai gallery Ayyam’s booth of the Dutch-Iraqi artist Sadik Kwaish Alfraiji. By the opening day, the Rafi works were about half sold.

Other Dubai galleries, who had a strong showing at the fair, equally did well, with Lawrie Shabibi selling out its marble inlay works by Hamra Abbas by the opening day for $50,000 each; Zawyeh Gallery selling about half of its collages by the Gazan artist Mohammed Joha, which had attracted much attention this year at the Venice Biennale; and Tabari Artspace, which showed two early works by another artist born in Gaza, Hazem Harb, amidst a group show, also reported selling half their booth. Most artworks were priced in the region of ten-thousands to mid-hundred thousand dollars.

A mix of blue-chip Western galleries were also in attendance. Pace were offering their fresh-to-market, large-scale paintings by the indigenous Australian artist Emily Kame Kngwarreye for between $80,000 to $750,000, although confirmed sales for these works appeared to be slow.

And in the small Frieze Masters section, a 2,000-year-old funerary stele made out of luminous alabaster, taken by a British official from what is now Yemen, was sold by the Mayfair gallerist David Aaron for "seven figures".

There were also a substantial number of new visitors to the fair, including a few starry faces like the tennis star Venus Williams. A smattering of museum heads and curators from the US, Asia and Europe also flew in, such as Michael Govan of Lacma (who was speaking at the fair), Eugene Tan of the Singapore Art Museum, and the Aspen Art Museum’s Nicola Lees, one of a number who brought along a patrons group.

And though the fair also had a number of South Asian galleries, Indian and Pakistani collectors were less present than expected, partly because the fair came right on the heels of Art Mumbai.

Perhaps as importantly, most galleries reported selling to these new collectors—both to collectors who had flown in as well as new collectors living in Abu Dhabi. The city’s population has swelled recently, particularly in the finance and tech sectors, in addition to the surge of Russians who moved to the UAE after the 2022 restrictions imposed on their country.

But the larger context of regional instability could not be ignored. Though it was hard to say how many people had stayed away because of fears of a resumption in Iran’s attacks on the UAE, it is undeniable that the frothy hype of a year ago, when the Art Basel/Doha and DCT/Abu Dhabi partnerships were announced, has settled for now. There was some sense of the fair’s energy being a product of solidarity—one collector from Beirut noted that Art Basel Paris closed early because of threats of riots, whereas the Arab art scene was pulling together under keener threats. But it would be more accurate to say that most people felt the need to get on with things rather than waiting for some far-off resolution.

This applies too for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which is scheduled to open next month after twenty years in the making. While the imminent opening partly detracted from the fair—some VIPs saw a choice between attending the fair and the early December festivities—the finished building and the buoyant museum team contributed to a sense of anticipation and substance within Abu Dhabi’s art scene.

High-level VIP tours got a preview of the building, The Art Newspaper understands, while the general VIP program was padded out with tours of the recently opened Public Art Abu Dhabi biennial, the Nomad art fair, and shows at the Cultural Foundation, the Bassam Freiha Art Foundation, and 421, as well as a number of private collections in the city—an itinerary that the city could not have supported even five years ago.

What was less visible on the trip, however, was commercial galleries. These remain almost exclusively in Dubai and fostering an independent commercial scene is a key reason for DCT’s partnership with Frieze, and also animates the city’s development of two new cultural districts, Noma on Saadiyat, led by the developer Aldar, and MiZa in Mina Zayed, led by the Sheikha Salama Foundation.

Both of these areas promise infrastructure to support artists and creative freelancers, such as studios, galleries, and co-working spaces.

These offerings will entail a loosening of control over the cultural programme in the city and—as is the case with Frieze—partnerships with private enterprise. For many who have followed the scene for a long time, this transition towards multiple stakeholders will be a key test for the capital.

“What Abu Dhabi has been doing over the last two decades is building an ecosystem, and one that is not solely institutional, but which also includes academia and smaller art spaces like 421,” says Aaron Cesar, the director of London’s Delfina Foundation. “There is now a clear path for the development of patrons and collectors—still in the making but a real possibility now, with MiZa and Noma to help complete the process. But Abu Dhabi can only do this through partnerships between public/private—that is, if they allow the voices of artists, designers, writers, and curators to come to the table with those who have money and power.”

The area, called Noma, will be near the site of the first Frieze Abu Dhabi, which launches next month in the Saadiyat Cultural District

Taking over the longstanding Abu Dhabi Art, the Frieze brand has lured international dealerships alongside a strong showing of regional names

Building on more than two decades of development in the UAE, Frieze’s first Middle East fair seeks to promote regional artists and boost Abu Dhabi’s reputation as a destination for global elites

The founder of Rizq Art Initiative is determined to support—and diversify—the local art scene

#9294. The Paradox of “Finding Yourself”

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

You can also become a spontaneous supporter with a one-time donation in any amount:

Partial to Bitcoin? You can beam some bit-love my way: 197usDS6AsL9wDKxtGM6xaWjmR5ejgqem7

Need to cancel a recurring donation? Go here.

For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

“No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself. And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan so brilliantly satirized and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness, completely illusory in its solidity.

Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry (public library) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society.

Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes:

In the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time.

In consonance with my own deep belief in the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming, Warren adds:

The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that “poems are physical sites of discovery [and] sense-records of our humanity,” Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being:

How does poetry come into all this? By being an antidote, a sovereign antidote, for passivity. For the basic fact about poetry is that it demands participation, from the secret physical echo in muscle and nerve that identifies us with the medium, to the imaginative enactment that stirs the deepest recesses where life-will and values reside. Beyond that, it nourishes our life-will in the process of testing our values. And this is not to be taken as implying a utilitarian aesthetic. It is, rather, one way of describing our pleasure in poetry as an adventure in the celebration of life.

Complement this particular portion of Warren’s thoroughly transcendent Democracy and Poetry with Walt Whitman on identity and the paradox of the self and philosopher Rebecca Goldstein on what makes you and your childhood self the “same” person despite a lifetime of change, then revisit Elizabeth Alexander on what poetry does for the human spirit.

#9293. Is Conspiracy Thinking in the Person or the Place?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Here are three statements. How much do you agree with each?

Food should be chosen based on each person's blood group.

Evidence of alien contact is being concealed from the public.

These seem to have little in common, but people who agree with one tend to agree with the others (Lobato and colleagues, 2014).

All three statements come from questionnaires that measure what researchers call epistemically suspect beliefs: confident claims about how the world works that go beyond, or against, the available evidence.

Because these beliefs hang together so well, many researchers treat them as something close to a personality trait, a stable way of seeing things. Others see them as a response to the world. Conspiracy theories, for example, tend to spread during periods of social crisis (van Prooijen and Douglas, 2017).

If these beliefs are traits, they should stay roughly the same from year to year, regardless of what happens around a person. A response to the world would instead rise and fall as people’s view of that world changes. Most studies cannot tell which is true, because they measure people only once.

In a paper just published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, my colleagues and I tested the two views (Alper and colleagues, 2026). The project, led by Sinan Alper of Yaşar University. was funded by TÜBİTAK, Türkiye's national science agency.

We surveyed the same adults in Türkiye and the United Kingdom five times, once every six months. At the start, 2,077 people participated in Türkiye and 959 in the UK. Each time, they reported these beliefs and rated corruption among public officials, business executives, and the media, as well as other attitudes.

The two countries differ sharply on corruption. On Transparency International’s (2026) Corruption Perceptions Index, the UK ranks 20th of 182 countries, and Türkiye ranks 124th.

On average, the beliefs declined slightly over the two years, except for conspiracy belief in Türkiye, which showed no clear change. I wouldn't read much into this, since answering the same questions repeatedly can itself lower scores. What struck me more was how tightly linked the three beliefs were. At the start, the correlations between them were strong, ranging from .65 to .86. Change was linked even more tightly. When a person’s belief in the paranormal fell, their belief in pseudoscience and conspiracy theories tended to fall with it.

One possibility is that all three reflect a single underlying tendency. Simpler explanations, such as people answering the survey less carefully over time, cannot yet be ruled out. Either way, much of the change is shared, but not all of it.

In Türkiye, people who saw more corruption over the past two years also became more open to conspiracy theories. Their paranormal and pseudoscientific beliefs did not follow. In the UK, we found no such link.

This may seem to clash with the previous section, and in part it does. Most of the change in these beliefs is shared, but each may keep some room to move on its own. In Türkiye, corruption may have tracked the portion attributable to conspiracy beliefs alone. It makes sense that belief in conspiracy was the one to move. A conspiracy theory claims that powerful people are secretly working together for their own gain. Corruption is often a true version of that story. Black cats and blood-type diets have nothing to do with it.

At the start of the study, though, the link between perceived corruption and conspiracy belief was about twice as strong in the UK (r = .61) as in Türkiye (r = .32). The difference may come down to how common corruption is. Where it is relatively rare, seeing it everywhere may say more about the person than about the country and may function as a stable trait. Where corruption is widespread and changing, people’s sense of it may follow those changes, and conspiracy beliefs may shift accordingly.

Our answer is both. These beliefs are steady and hang together, but they can still change.

Some factors seem to set a person’s starting point. People higher in authoritarianism, who value discipline and following leaders in unity, endorsed all three kinds of beliefs more in both countries. But changes in authoritarianism did not track changes in belief. Perceived corruption works differently, and whether it moves these beliefs seems to depend on where you live.

This fits earlier work. Conspiracy beliefs are more common in countries with widespread corruption and in less stable societies, where education offers less protection against them (Alper, 2023). In another study I coauthored, education was also less tied to trust in science in highly corrupt countries (Alper and colleagues, 2024). In such places, people might learn to distrust authority from experience.

When someone you know shares a conspiracy theory, ask two questions. Is this how they see everything, from health advice to the evening news? Or is it a response to something they have watched go wrong? The first kind of belief tends to change slowly. The second should be taken seriously, because sometimes suspicion points at something real.

Careful thinking still matters. In a recent experiment, my colleagues and I found that training designed to encourage reflection lowered conspiracy beliefs (Bayrak and colleagues, 2025). But when institutions keep giving people reasons to be suspicious, better thinking can only do so much. I guess that in some places the best answer to conspiracy thinking is institutions that give people less to suspect. Survey data like ours cannot settle that.

Sinan Alper and I have begun to test it experimentally. In two preregistered studies with nationally representative US samples, we described an unnamed US state or a fictional country as either highly corrupt or very clean (Alper and Yilmaz, 2026).

People found conspiracy claims about the corrupt place far more believable, and this was most closely tied to a sense that resources were being shared unfairly. The paper is still under peer review, and I will write about it once it is done.

Alper, S., Konukoglu, K., Bayrak, F., Yener, C., Bagci, E. S., Dogruyol, B., & Yilmaz, O. (2026). Stable worldviews or context-sensitive systems? Longitudinal evidence on the development of epistemically suspect beliefs across two sociopolitical contexts. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672261463908

Alper, S., Yelbuz, B. E., Akkurt, S. B., & Yilmaz, O. (2024). The positive association of education with the trust in science and scientists is weaker in highly corrupt countries. Public Understanding of Science, 33(1), 2–19. https://doi.org/10.1177/09636625231176935

Alper, S., & Yilmaz, O. (2026, June 11). Corruption cues increase conspiracy beliefs: the central role of perceived distributive fairness. Retrieved from osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/jfr4n_v1

Bayrak, F., Sümer, V., Dogruyol, B., Saribay, S. A., Alper, S., Isler, O., & Yilmaz, O. (2025). Reflection predicts and leads to decreased conspiracy belief. Cognition, 258, 106085. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2025.106085

Lobato, E., Mendoza, J., Sims, V., & Chin, M. (2014). Examining the relationship between conspiracy theories, paranormal beliefs, and pseudoscience acceptance among a university population. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 28(5), 617–625. https://doi.org/10.1002/acp.3042

#9292. What China Taught Me About America's Rambunctious Streak

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

I've long wondered whether a rambunctious toddler is more likely to develop a balanced temperament than a reticent tike. Is a quiet kid more likely to learn boldness than a bold child is to learn when to shut up?

I bring that up because, having just visited China, I've been thinking about the trajectories of our almost opposite nations.

The Chinese are a much more cooperative population than we are. It shows up even in the fluid dynamics of the society.

I spent a lot of time walking through non-touristy streets. That's not enough to make me an expert, but I did form impressions. People flow around each other more fluidly than they do here. They're not distracted by each other. They don't nod or look each other in the eye. They simply assume each other. There seems to be no stigma in being glued to a phone.

They're less thirsty for attention. They aren't busy reassuring each other or trying to stand out. They strain less to look and feel exceptional. There were plenty of stylish young people, but not to the extent we see here. Even the ads are less glam.

It stands to reason. This is a huge, dense urban population whose parents and grandparents, a generation or two ago, were mostly peasants. Their society was shaped by Confucianism 2,500 years ago, a philosophy that is more about etiquette than anything else, at least in its popular form.

Yes, the Chinese have at times gone terribly off the rails. Indonesia also struck me as an extraordinarily tolerant society, yet 60 years ago anti-Communists there slaughtered over a million people. Societies can change. But today China is a mild child. We're the thirsty, intense, fanatical, exceptionalist, rambunctious one.

We distract ourselves with obscene amounts of self-flattery and pandering in commerce and politics. The midterms alone cost 12 billion dollars. All that pandering and flattery doesn't make us wiser. It makes us more anxious and delusional.

We've just about used up the earth's carrying capacity for self-flattering nonsense. Meanwhile, the demand for flattery and pandering is only getting worse.

In China, there's so little of it, at least so far. That could change, as it did in Indonesia after I visited eight years ago, with the rise of Islamic fundamentalism.

China doesn't go through the motions of national elections. It's one-party rule, with no pandering and a focus on practical welfare that, on my visit, went far beyond what we see here. They plan to double their train lines by 2035. There's practically no theft in the city center, and the cameras are everywhere, so you'd get caught and punished. China's Gini coefficient, a measure of wealth inequality, is around 35. Ours is about ten points higher.

On my two trips there, I met only one Christian. It's an atheist country, and you can't talk about the supernatural as real. There's none of our jersey-wearing, lifestyle-brand supernaturalist grandstanding and infighting.

People grumble about the lack of freedom of speech, but they can grumble without looking over their shoulders. At Peking University, built on the land of the emperor's Summer Palace and just a few blocks from the government center, a professor told me that, paradoxically, they have more freedom of speech there. In distant cities, you have to attend a Communist Party meeting every two weeks. At the university, you just fill out minutes. There are limits, though. You can't talk casually about Mao on social media, and you can't call him a dictator. They're trying to put the violence of the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution behind them, along with the poverty. In 1976, China's average income was a third of Sub-Saharan Africa's. They've come a long way. Maybe they'll keep going.

If you're not watching China, you should be. Odds are they will surpass us, and Pax Americana will give way to Pax Sinica. Since I study American fanaticism, I could get a distorted view of humankind. China makes me think humankind might pull off some kind of harmony. It fills me with optimism about human potential.

And maybe we'll learn from China's success. Maybe the rambunctious child will learn to chill out. We had better.

Maybe we'll converge on some mix of reticent and rambunctious that makes humankind survivable.

Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable, that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage.

Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop, the golden fan of the gingko, the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe.

In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is.

Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive.

Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.”

What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”).

If you have sat in the chill of early morning bleakness

and watched as the deep blue sighed and blushed, touched

by the warm curve of dawn and pinker than pink then

apricot soft and spreading its glow, you know. You know.

How — in this dim parade of brutality — might all be well?

But if we trouble it with light, train our sights on the rebellious good,

In the chapter called lostness, a friend.

It cannot be always comfortable. So love the thousand knives as they enter and see your shape still sitting.

See that you too belong to paws of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled roots, to silver-spun constellations.

Know you’re no sicker than the rest of us. The big secret is this: No one else can brave you. Messy, yes. And marvelous.

What is more than we see in this world we’re pressed into, its blistered barking noise?

For what we build, speak, and ruin — our efforts, our angers.

#9290. Like Fine Wine, Life Can Improve With Age

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Aging reflects shared humanity; we are all in this together. Yet perceived purpose in life is a factor that we can improve. Research explores how to forge a positive path forward at any age.

Yiqing Yang and Kelin Li (2026) explored pathways to perceiving aging in older adults.[i] They acknowledge that self-perceptions of aging (SPA), defined as personal experiences, beliefs, and evaluations of the aging process, predict behavioral health outcomes as people grow older. Encompassing both positive and negative assessments, SPAs include perceptions of purpose, growth, and resilience, as well as concerns about physical, mental, or social decline. Yang and Li note that people experience aging differently, some seeing a decline in energy or physical ability while others enjoy improved emotional regulation. Not surprisingly, they recognize SPA as a robust predictor of physical and mental health, cognitive functioning, health-related behavior, and longevity.

Studying a racially diverse sample of adults aged 65 and older, Yang and Li identified some positive and negative predictors of SPA. One of the most significant was purpose in life, which consistently predicted higher positive SPA and lower negative SPA, making it an essential psychological resource over time. They note that purpose in life may prompt both meaning and direction, supporting an adaptive interpretation of aging. Accordingly, purpose can be viewed as an accumulated asset that may help older adults see aging as continuous growth as opposed to inevitable decline. This reframing can also protect against what Yang and Li refer to as internalized age stereotypes through maintaining a forward-looking orientation, counteracting age-related loss or perceived constraints.

Yang and Li note that their results also emphasize the concept of SPA as multidimensional. Positive SPA was linked with psychological strengths such as life satisfaction, purpose, and self-esteem, as well as a robust social life and religious affiliation. They interpret these findings as suggesting that maintaining a favorable view of aging is developed through psychological well-being, meaningful social engagement, and a sense of belonging. They contrast these positive outcomes with negative SPA, which was linked with negative outcomes such as having a limited social network, perceived constraints, more health problems, and higher religiosity, indicating that negative perceptions of aging may be explained less by the lack of resources than by perceptions of restrictions, loss, and declining autonomy.

Yang and Li advise caution when interpreting their findings regarding religious involvement. They observe that religious affiliation produces social connection and identity benefits that bolster positive views about aging, although a higher degree of religiosity may suggest different coping styles and responses to stress or health challenges that are linked to negative SPA. They therefore acknowledge the importance of assessing multiple dimensions of individual religious involvement, as opposed to viewing spirituality as a single construct. This advice is consistent with the reality that different religions have different belief systems, including views of the afterlife, which will effect older people differently than their younger counterparts.

Celebrating purpose in life can promote adaptive attitudes about aging and mitigate negative self-perception. It is never too late to be thankful for your circumstances, including faith, family, and friends, as well as your ability to continue to grow emotionally and spiritually. By taking stock of your blessings, which include not only worldly wealth but wisdom, you can refresh and renew a sense of purpose in life, as well as health, happiness, and hope for the future.

[i] Yang, Yiqing, and Kelin Li. “Psychosocial Resources and Constraints: Distinct Pathways to Positive and Negative Self-Perceptions of Aging in Diverse Older Adults.” Clinical Gerontologist: The Journal of Aging and Mental Health, May 11, 2026.

#9289. Men of Pause: Redefining Manhood Through Vasectomy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

December 2014. She had just come out of an emergency C-section with our daughter. She was still shaking on the recovery table. She looked at me and said: “I'm done.”

She wasn't asking. She wasn't pushing me. She was just done.

September 2019. Galit needed to replace her IUD. This time, for the first time, we actually had an open discussion about it. Why does she need to take sole responsibility for birth control for both of us? I started considering a vasectomy. But I was scared. Not of the procedure. Scared of what it meant. Scared to close that chapter. Scared to end the part of me that was still, biologically, a man with options.

We researched, met a urologist, but ultimately, at the last minute, I bailed. Galit was happy that at least we spoke about it openly.

February 2026. I finally had my vasectomy.

The first time someone cut that part of my body, I was eight days old. I didn't choose it. I was ushered into a covenant, a tradition. This happened before I could speak, before I could consent, before I even knew I had a body.

That is how it goes for most men. The first major act performed on our reproductive organ happens without our permission. We enter the tribe like everyone else. Unaware. Another boy marked into the tribe.

For many of us, that pattern continues. Sex gets socialized into us as performance, as conquest, as something we take. Reproduction becomes the measure of our masculinity. Our job is to spread our seed. We are procreators. That is our identity. So when the vasectomy conversation comes up, most men hear one thing: Loss. That’s how I felt back then.

I want to suggest the opposite: A vasectomy doesn’t hurt your masculinity, it actually liberates you.

Some men hear the word vasectomy and their stomach tightens. It sounds like castration. Like a punishment.

I understand that feeling. Anything that touches that part of us is triggering. That part is the symbol for what we learn is our worth, our trophy, our uniqueness. Limiting or “damaging” it threatens our sense of manhood.

But this is different. This time you have agency. This is a choice you make. You decide what happens to your body. Not your parents. Not your religion.

In a way, vasectomy is a form of positive liberty. The first circumcision wasn’t your choice. Someone chose for you. The second one was made of your free choice. You choose it because you want to.

Isaiah Berlin called this positive liberty. By choosing the second cut, you gain the (positive) freedom to live your life according to your values.

Here’s what I didn’t expect. It’s been about 9 months since the operation and nothing has changed. Not physically. Not sexually. Not sensually. To be honest, my body feels like the procedure never happened.

The only thing that changed is how I see myself.

It was a symbolic circumcision. A symbolic change.

Maybe I'm entering another tribe now. A tribe of older men who are ready to initiate others, because it is no longer about me.

This is the threshold we wrote about in the relational hero's journey. Once he crosses the point of no return, he embarks on a journey, which will change him forever. He will return ‘home’, a wiser hero, bringing his new wisdom and abilities to change the world.

This is also what middle age has been teaching me. The focus shifts. From spreading the seed to serving others. From building my own life to initiating the men coming up behind me. Guiding men into mature, differentiated manhood. The books Iron John and The New Manhood teach us that the older man's task is not to keep proving himself. It is to initiate the younger ones. To age and to sage. A vasectomy, for me, was one way of stepping into that.

I call this being a man of pause. To pause, reflect, and take the time to care for others.

There is a principle screenwriting teacher Robert McKee returns to. The artist becomes more creative inside their limitation not outside it. I have felt this everywhere. Writing a PhD inside its rules. Training for a marathon within the plan. Learning to touch my wife the way she wants in a 30-day challenge. The limit is what helped me be better.

The vasectomy is a creative limitation. I blocked one dimension of my sexuality, the reproductive one, and what I got back was focus. Energy that is no longer worried about an unwanted pregnancy. Energy I can channel somewhere else. Toward my marriage, my art, my clinical work. Toward changing the world in the years I have left.

We fixate on what we will not be able to do anymore. The better question is what this limitation will open up? When you close the door on your reproduction, what new vista will appear?

I am not telling you to get a vasectomy. That is between you and your partner. I am asking you something else. I'm asking you to ask yourself:

Where in your life are you willing to cut something off?

Where do you dare to block one dimension of you, so you can evolve into the next version of yourself?

Where and how are you ready to evolve your manhood?

If men stopped thinking about themselves, put their ego aside, and turned toward service, that would change the world.

When you were a baby, someone made that choice for you.

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D.-candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

Berlin, I. (1969). Two concepts of liberty. In Four essays on liberty (pp. 118–172). Oxford University Press.

Biddulph, S. (2014). The new manhood. Finch Publishing.

Bly, R. (1990). Iron John: A book about men. Addison-Wesley.

McKee, R. (1997). Story: Substance, structure, style, and the principles of screenwriting. ReganBooks.

#9288. Flooding in southwestern US underlines risks of Trump administration’s reduction of Bears Ears National Monument

The Newspaper Rock petroglyphs are among the archaeological sites within Bears Ears National Monument in Utah Photo: Matthew Dillon, via Flickr

Recent catastrophic flooding across the southwestern US has renewed concerns about the future management and preservation of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah, which is home to a rich concentration of archaeological sites. The concerns follow the Trump administration’s decision to reduce the monument from more than one million acres to around 120,000 acres, reversing Biden-era protections and dismantling its Indigenous-led management structure.

The decision to shrink the boundaries of the protected area and open the site to resource extraction has become a flashpoint as the region grapples with the effects of severe weather, with the recent floods raising questions around the resources available for the preservation of heritage sites. The flooding hit the Four Corners area—which encompasses parts of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah—from late October to early November, causing widespread damage to roads and infrastructure.

A spokesperson for the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) Monticello field office in southeastern Utah says in a statement to The Art Newspaper that the public lands it manages, which includes Bears Ears National Monument, were significantly affected by flash floods, resulting in major washouts on many primary access roads and rendering some routes impassable. BLM staff have been patrolling the region to assess road conditions and evaluate the status of infrastructure around areas used for recreation.

“Park rangers and archaeologists have also been assessing cultural sites to identify any potential impacts from the flooding,” the spokesperson says. “While storm events of this nature are not uncommon in this landscape and can affect sensitive cultural resources, no immediate impacts on cultural sites have been reported at this time.”

The local researcher and author Ralph “R.E.” Burrillo was in the town of Bluff, Utah, a gateway to Bears Ears National Monument, when the floods started in late October. He notes that the management plan for the new boundaries has not yet been implemented, so nothing has changed other than the “invisible line”. The longer-term implications, however, remain uncertain.

“With a monument in place, there wouldn’t be these wildcat permits for people supposedly looking to extract resources, but these are just exploratory leases,” he says. “The reality is that there isn’t that much energy to be extracted underground in Bears Ears, or people would have been going after it for decades. When anybody says the monument is locking up America’s energy potential, they are lying.”

Other monuments in the region, like the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in southern Utah, which has substantial deposits of coal and other minerals like uranium, chromium and copper, have a longer history of conflict over resource extraction. The Clinton administration established the monument in 1996 in part to prevent commercial development of coal extraction. Several companies had acquired coal leases in the region during the 1960s and 70s, although commercial mining never materialised.

Burrillo emphasises that the demarcation of the Bears Ears National Monument benefits two constituencies: resource developers and opponents of tribal stewardship. The Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and the Bears Ears National Monument are frequently reduced due to a “handshake deal” that grants energy lobbyists access to energy resources from one site and removes tribal jurisdiction from the latter. At this time, the main immediate threat to heritage sites in the region, Burrillo adds, remains tourism, looting and vandalism.

“What the monument did, at least potentially, was create a nexus for funding to be sent to that area for things like interdiction and law enforcement, education and interpretation, trail maintenance and collaboration with tribes,” Burrillo says. “A monument is a conduit for funding to try to protect those resources from vandals, looters and, again, tourists, who, whether intentionally or not, crawl all over the place. Without the monument, there’s no nexus for funding and that’s really a knock-on effect.”

Although flooding could affect archaeological sites, including potentially eroding petroglyphs, Burrillo says that prehistoric sites in the region are of the least concern. The region has historically flooded, with water sometimes rising to 50ft, and its archaeological sites tell a fascinating story of adaptability, with sites like ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings having been built higher than the water could ever reach. When Mormon pioneers arrived in the region in the 1870s and attempted to establish a town at Bluff, with farms and as an outpost for missioning the Navajo population, they were unsuccessful and eventually moved north.

“When you go back 500 to 2,000 years, the people didn’t have those dams. You simply had this tempestuous river that was famous for flooding more or less constantly, filling miles around the flood basin with water and mud,” Burrillo adds. “The ancestral Pueblo and their ancestors knew it and built above it. For the most part, they treated the river with more respect than we have. The archaeology is in far less danger than the modern infrastructure for that reason.”

Opponents of the plan say Nine Mile Canyon, described as “the world’s longest art gallery”, is too narrow and fragile to accommodate the widened road and increased tanker traffic

The governance and size of the monument have been disputed for years, and Utah Republicans are still trying to block president Biden's 2021 expansion of its boundaries

The Bureau of Land Management is offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of those responsible

Legislators in the state are planning legal action in order to allow mining in region that contains 100,000 archaeological sites

#9287. The Third Thing: Poet Donald Hall on the Secret to Lasting Love

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood.
