#9250. US affordable artists' housing initiatives hobbled by uneven regulation and oversight

Artist Emilie Dundee Odeile has exhibited at a state-subsidised arts project in Trinidad, Colorado Courtesy Dundee & Lee

“Affordability” is on the lips of every American. In Colorado, over 35% of residents spend more than 30% of their income on housing, which is considered a cost burden by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (Hud). The state is responding by allocating $300m annually to the State Affordable Housing Fund. A niche area of this investment is the development of affordable housing for artists and creative districts.

National non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort. Both non-profits market affordable housing for artists, but in the absence of artist certification programmes such as those in Boston, New York and now San Francisco, restricting available affordable housing to artists could run the risk of violating fair housing laws. There are also few mechanisms for cities and states to ensure their public funding delivers long-term solutions for artists’ housing and creative spaces.

“We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border. The artists used around 152 miles of yarn to bring the famous children’s book to life in a 2023 exhibition.

“We started our RV-life, one-year road trip experiment,” Chapin says. “We were on our way to Santa Fe, and went through Trinidad”—and they never left. Goodnight Moon and another project by Odeile debuted at Space to Create, a state-led initiative to produce creative workforce housing and studios in rural Colorado.

Trinidad was the first municipality identified by the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade (OEDIT) for public investment through the establishment of a creative district, in 2015. Today, 37 creative districts exist across the state. Next door to Space to Create on Trinidad’s historic Main Street, Artspace manages residences for artists.

Artspace develops and operates workforce housing across 23 states, including seven projects in Colorado. Each project markets itself “for those in the creative sector” and offers residential space that “prioritises creative use”. But without a formal certification programme to identify artists in Colorado or any of the local municipalities it operates in, it is unclear how Artspace can legally give preference to artist applicants over members of the general public.

Poet and editor Michele McDannold lived in Artspace’s complex in Michigan City, Indiana, for nearly four years and at the organisation’s Honolulu location for seven months. She arrived in Trinidad in 2020, but noticed a substantial difference in the artist preference process at that location compared to the properties she had been in previously. In Michigan City, she says, “I had to give a presentation to a board of practicing artists and participate in an interview.” In Trinidad, she was only asked to submit information for income eligibility. McDannold has only encountered five artists across the property’s 40 units during her three-year stay. The result of not prioritising artist applicants appeared to be that there were almost no artist residents.

“When it came time to organise or participate in something like [open studios or a gallery night],” McDannold says, “neighbours were like, ‘What? Why are you bothering me?”

Artspace did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s multiple requests for comment. The Artspace Trinidad leasing office stated that it does not track the number of artist residents at that location.

Affordable housing is a broad term that lives on a spectrum of interpretation and regulation. According to the federal government, household affordability is based on the regional or area median income (AMI). What a property owner can charge a tenant is determined by Hud’s AMI calculations, but a lender can set the contractual terms of the tax credit, loan or grant, whether private or public. Under US Treasury regulations, a housing unit generates a low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) only if it is available for general-public use. However, in 2008 the Housing and Economic Recovery Act added a provision to the Internal Revenue Service’s tax code stating that general-public use is not violated if preference is given to tenants involved in artistic or literary activities. Even so, some cities maintain their own artist certification programmes for affordable housing.

A 2023 affordable housing audit by Denver’s Department of Housing Stability expressed concerns that priority access to housing could violate the federal Fair Housing Act. While the report specifically focused on the Denver city council’s move to prioritise displaced households or people at risk of displacement, it highlighted the fact that prioritising seniors and veterans also requires better systems for monitoring and evaluation. Each time a person, such as an artist, is prioritised for affordable housing access, the county must track data such as the number of units allocated, eligibility requirements, types of document accepted as evidence of eligibility, the selection process, and the parties responsible for implementation and monitoring the property and rent levels.

Municipal governments are concerned about incurring fair housing lawsuits, especially if state and county laws contradict or fail to reaffirm the 2008 tax code revision. Cities considering allocating affordable housing units for artists can be faced with having to develop significant compliance procedures. This patchwork of rules, requirements and compliance regimes helps explain why creating and maintaining affordable housing for artists can be very complicated, costly, and look different in different cities and regions. According to the Center for an Urban Future, US cities have created just 2,804 units of dedicated housing for artists in the last decade.

The soaring windows of 210 East Street in Trinidad must have caught the eye of the developer Dana Crawford when she first visited the elegant century-old school building. Crawford, who died in January 2025, was a celebrated preservationist in the region, known for saving Denver’s historic Larimer Square and redeveloping the city’s Union Station. There were minimal requirements attached to the $4m community revitalisation grant Crawford received for the redevelopment of 210 East Street into 17 affordable live-work spaces for artists. An open records request reveals the terms of the grant for the property only ask for progress reports on the number of housing units and jobs created.

The Former East Street School building in Trinidad, Colorado has been converted to housing and marketed as affordable for artists, among others Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust

For the 210 East Street project, Crawford procured three different tax credits, the $4m community revitalisation grant and $1.8m in private financing, but the most restrictive terms were attached to last-minute funding from the city of Trinidad. In 2022 Crawford applied to the city’s Housing Now incentive programme to help cover the $125,000 cost of redesigning five units. The city approved the request on the condition of a two-year workforce housing deed restriction, requiring rent rates to be limited to 80% of AMI starting in 2023.

Crawford also sought $1.9m in funding from an impact investor, Greenland CDF. The funding from Greenland was contingent on signing a Community Benefit Agreement (CBA), a binding contract that requires the borrower to produce a social benefit with enforceable penalties. The details of the agreement are not public and expired earlier this year.

Less than five years after Crawford received a total of $7.5m in public funding for 210 East Street, the property was acquired by Cast. There are no existing public terms that legally require Cast to deliver affordable housing to artists, or even general housing.

Cast operates a non-profit real estate development strategy around creative spaces and affordability. Recently, the organisation expanded that strategy to housing in Colorado.

“Our model as a non-profit is to reset the floor of affordability,” says Ken Ikeda, Cast’s chief executive. “If we could do that without debt, through grants, then that would keep it that way in perpetuity.”

Currently, Ikeda adds, Cast is only required to deliver the private terms of the $1.9m grant the organisation received from the Colorado Health Foundation to acquire 210 East Street. Rent at the complex is currently between 55% and 80% of AMI, and according to a spokesperson for the organisation, five current residents are artists. The Art Newspaper was only able to verify that one resident is an artist, and that person said they know of no others.

Half a mile from 210 East Street are three properties that have received significant public funding in exchange for affordable artists’ housing. In 2019 ownership of two addresses on Main Street and one on Elm Street were transferred to Artspace by the city of Trinidad. In exchange for that real estate and a $715,000 promissory note by the Colorado Housing Finance Authority in 2022, Artspace must deliver housing units within or below 40% to 60% of AMI for 35 years, and preserve the historic facade of the Main Street properties for 15 years. If it fails to maintain this commitment, it must repay the borrowed funds.

The vastly different requirements for the Artspace and Cast properties in Trinidad, and the strings attached (or not) to their public and private funding reflect the wildly different standards and requirements for organisations creating and operating affordable artists’ housing.

The 444 17th Street building in Denver, the future site of a multi-use affordable housing and cultural hub for artists, to be operated by Community Arts Stabilization Trust Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust

A vibrant art and culture scene boosts local businesses and helps create jobs, according to the Denver Downtown Development Authority (DDDA), a city initiative to revive a downtown core where the vacancy rate has remained at or above 30% since the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2025 and 2026 the DDDA awarded $114.5m in financing for new housing and $4.45m for art-related initiatives—including a $1.35m grant to Cast to convert 6,300 sq. ft of vacant office and retail space into affordable artists’ studios, a cinema and gallery. The city council approved the terms of the property’s sale to Cast in September.

“We are going to make it affordable no matter what, because that is our aim and objective,” Ikeda says of the project in Denver, which has been vacant since 2021. Cast estimates the art space will open in the summer of 2027.

Representatives for the city did not clarify how it defines “affordable” in the context of commercial real estate, but noted that the city has the first right to purchase the property for $1 for the next ten years if Cast decides to sell. In the meantime, municipal support will be released in phases as Cast reaches a series of build-out milestones.

While Denver finds its footing on affordable housing for artists and New York has not added any units in a decade, San Francisco’s first dedicated affordable artists’ housing is on track to open in 2028. The Artist Hub on Market, at 1687 Market Street, will have 94 units of housing, rehearsal space and a theatre. Rent will be set between 30% and 80% of the AMI, depending on the size of the unit and number of occupants, which equates to annual income of between $46,440 and $167,120 for tenants.

A rendering of the future Artists Hub on Market project in San Francisco Courtesy Artists Hub on Market and Mercy Housing California

Launching alongside the Market Street property is a new artist certification programme for San Francisco, facilitated by the Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development. Artists can achieve certification by documenting at least $10,000 in annual income from their art practice, showing proof of a public art commission or grant in the previous three years, or submitting a portfolio of work for review. Once certification is awarded, artists can enter the lottery for units at Artist Hub on Market; any units unclaimed by artists in the lottery will be opened to general-public use through the city’s affordable housing system.

Of the Artist Hub on Market project’s $140m in funding, $100m came from a single anonymous donor and, according to a source familiar with the terms of the deal, implementing the artist certification programme was a condition of the funding.

The inconsistent regulation of properties that receive public funding for affordable artists’ housing and cultural spaces risks undermining such projects’ longevity and disappointing the communities they were meant to serve. Recently, a $400,000 low-interest loan from the DDDA to Denver Immersive Repertory Theater (Dirt) went into default after Dirt’s alleged failure to make rent payments less than a year after it was awarded the loan and before its project ever opened to the public. According to reporting by Denverite, the loan’s rate surges from 3% to 15% when loan proceeds are shown to not be used for their intended purpose, though it is unclear what assets the city will be able to claw back from the project’s founders.

Affordable housing for artists is an emerging sector entangled with various local governments’ goals, which include attracting business, lowering housing costs by adding units and retaining creative workers. Ikeda describes every affordability project as a funding “butterfly” due to the unique risks and complexity of the capital and terms assembled. But, he adds, they are worth the trouble: “There is something magical about artist-only housing and live-work environments.”

While it is not a central topic in their campaigns, Andrew Cuomo, Zohran Mamdani and Curtis Sliwa have all addressed issues relevant to artists and arts workers

Spaceworks’ initiatives span Brooklyn and the Bronx, but concerns are raised about their long-term impact

Those responsible for building Miami's vibrant art scene are struggling to pay for housing and workspaces

#9249. Thanksgiving Isn't Over Yet

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

There’s a riddle in Alain de Botton and John Armstrong’s book Art as Therapy: What’s the most important part of a museum?

Consider that for a second. Maybe it’s the architecture, the explainers on the wall, or the audio tour that helps you make sense of an abstract creation.

This is not about surrendering to late-stage capitalism or Black Friday consumerism: It’s about the importance of slowing down to take in the experience you just had. And following a holiday dedicated to gratitude, that’s why this weekend might be the most important part of Thanksgiving.

I love museums. They’re amazing places to take in ideas and beauty with other people. But after a world-expanding hour or two, we step back into traffic and chores and, little by little, the magic dissipates.

Enter the gift shop. It’s a chance to travel back in time, to revisit what you just saw and buy a little trinket to keep that experience with you.

That’s the argument for museum gift shops: you’ve just had a lovely experience, but unless you slow down to make meaning of it and take it with you, you risk missing some of its goodness.

Maybe you’ve noticed that Thanksgiving also goes by fast. After all the logistics, planning, meal prep, traveling, and settling in… blink, it’s over. But it doesn’t have to be over, at least not in our minds.

I suspect your Thanksgiving wasn’t perfect, but I imagine it had some lovely moments. Here’s one of mine:

On our way to visit my cousin’s family in rural Maryland, we learned that they’d lost power. When we got there, it was still out. So, looking for a way to finish cooking, my cousin’s two Gen Z kids and I ventured out in the pouring rain and gusty wind to find some propane (because, of course, they were out of that, too).

After two failed attempts (one store was out, and the other wouldn’t sell it to us because their power was also out), we miraculously found some at the dollar store. Somewhere in the middle of this little adventure, I found myself sitting in the backseat, expanding my musical horizons with Slayyyter and having a silly time with my cousin’s kids, who, I might add, were being responsible and safe drivers.

It’s the kind of moment that’s easy to miss: the joy of watching the people you love grow up and appreciating how easily we made the most of a power outage.

Oh, and I forgot to mention the best part. Literally the minute we walked in with a full propane tank, returning heroes that we were, the power came back on.

After writing Sometimes You Should Be Late, I’ve become even more fixated on the question of when experiences truly end.

Does yoga class end the moment 9 a.m. hits and we race out and unlock our phones? Or can we take a few minutes to luxuriate in savasana, bask in the glow of sweat, and appreciate that we took time to slow down?

It’s the same with the rest of our lives: we can slow down to complete an experience, or we can rush past it.

I used to do a lot more things back to back to back, at work, on weekends, and on vacation. Here’s what I noticed: sure, I did a lot of activities, but it was harder to fully appreciate them. As I write in my book: “If our timelines leave no room to appreciate the experience we’re having or the people we’re having it with, why bother?”

Slowing down helps us pay attention. It helps us, as psychologist Rick Hanson says, to “take in the good.” He explains that our brains are often like Teflon for positive experiences but magnets for negative ones. Slowing down with the positive helps us rebalance.

What’s particularly interesting about taking in the good is that we don’t have to do this during experiences; we can do it afterward, too.

Here’s the Turkey Day upshot: Thanksgiving Day is over, but the experience of it isn’t.

So, instead of just moving on to the next holiday plan, here’s my invitation: dedicate a little time this weekend to taking in the good of what just happened, muddling imperfectly and all.

The movie Ferris Bueller’s Day Off offers this reminder: “Life moves pretty fast. If you don’t stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

And here’s the thing: we do have a choice to slow things down at the end, or even a few days afterward, to bring a little more appreciation to the moments of our lives.

That could be a museum visit, a good book, or a day of gathering together—holiday traffic, TSA ground stops, and power outages be damned.

Perhaps the most important part of Thanksgiving is what we choose to do with the experience once it’s over.

Here’s me slowing down with my Thanksgiving gratitude: thanks to my lovely cousin Ann for hosting, for muddling through a Thanksgiving feast without power and keeping it all together, and for raising two responsible kids… er, adults!

#9248. Autoimmunity and the Stories Women Tell About Illness

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Sara Hirsh Bordo on chronic illness, inherited expectations, and what it costs to stop being the good girl.

For many women, being good has always meant being useful. Their sense of worth becomes tied to anticipating everyone else’s needs, taking responsibility for problems that aren’t theirs, and making sure no one is disappointed. Their own needs fall to the bottom of the list. Over time, it can become difficult to remember what it feels like to put themselves first.

What are we afraid will happen if we stop being who others expect us to be?

Sara Hirsh Bordo spent 15 years as a documentary filmmaker telling women’s stories before she began examining her own. Her experiences with serious illness led her to question the rules she’d been living by, and the result is her first book, Autoimmunity and the Good Girls. She calls herself a “recovering good girl.”

When we spoke, she kept returning to one question: What are we afraid will happen if we stop being who others expect us to be?

We all know the vocabulary. I should do more. I should be available. I should be able to manage all of it. Bordo thinks the shoulds are not where this starts.

“I don’t think the ‘shoulds’ come first. I think the fears come first,” Bordo says.

She describes the questions that can arise when we begin challenging expectations we’ve lived with for years: What will my family think? Will I disappoint someone? What happens if I become someone new—and what if I don’t like that person?

“I think that if you can survive incremental levels of disappointing other people, all of a sudden, there’s freedom that comes in the place of those pockets,” Bordo says.

For Bordo, recognizing those fears meant reconsidering the rules she’d built her life around. She began questioning the expectations she’d inherited and making room for new ways of thinking about herself and her relationships.

“I think that if you can survive incremental levels of disappointing other people, all of a sudden, there’s freedom that comes in the place of those pockets,” she says.

She also recognizes how deeply these fears can be passed down through generations. They’re not just her own, she explains, but part of the expectations she saw reflected in her mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother.

She said this the morning after a Zoom conversation with a book club of about 17 women of color, where the conversation about permission brought several of them to tears. The discussion prompted reflection on expectations and beliefs that some women had carried for decades.

Bordo’s question started with a pattern. The women around her who had been diagnosed with chronic or autoimmune conditions were all eldest or only daughters, herself included. At first, she assumed it was connected to birth order. So she and what she calls her “crack team of volunteers” started calling the CDC and the NIH. They found research about birth order and health in general, but nothing on autoimmune disease specifically.

She then conducted an informal survey of 300 women in the U.S. with autoimmune conditions, and 70 percent reported being eldest or only daughters.

She then conducted an informal survey of 300 women in the U.S. with autoimmune conditions, and 70 percent reported being eldest or only daughters. A few of the others wrote her personal notes describing how they’d taken on significant responsibility for others, despite not being the eldest or only daughter.

The survey was not a scientific study and had no comparison group, so the findings cannot establish a connection between birth order and autoimmune disease. But the notes stayed with her, because they pointed past birth order to something she describes as “heightened responsibility too soon.”

These observations also led Bordo to think differently about the relationship between personal experiences and physical health.

“Our body doesn’t just speak science, it speaks story,” Bordo says.

“Our body doesn’t just speak science, it speaks story,” Bordo says.

A doctor she names as Dr. Carmona then introduced her to epigenetics, the study of how changes in gene activity can occur without altering the underlying DNA sequence. She used it to map experiences from different chapters of her life against what her body might have been doing at the time. She is clear that this is her own framework and not a medical explanation. But it gave her a way to think about the body’s immune response in autoimmune disease, and about permission as the story we tell about who we’re allowed to be.

Permission, she told me, “is just the ground floor.”

To describe what it feels like when fear loosens, she reaches for a heist movie. She means it as a picture of how the change felt; she doesn’t claim it explains how autoimmune disease starts or ends.

“I feel like that level of fear and the power of fear is holding the space for freedom. And when freedom lives more than fear does, I think that’s when we are jackknifed into an immune system that actually starts almost unlocking itself. And then it’s like an Ocean’s Eleven scene. They’re opening the safe, and it’s like the inner workings of the safe, and the wheels are spinning, and then the doors are opening, and then that’s the image that I feel is happening in a body. You actually become sovereign enough, and brave enough, and self-permitted enough to choose for yourself first, and other people second. That’s the shift.”

I told her that last line made me think of someone I know. She’s smart, she knows what she wants, and she keeps handing the decision back to the good girl. The story about what she should do wins out over her own happiness more often than not. I can watch it from the outside, going in circles.

Bordo shared an example from earlier that morning. Her best friend’s mother was dying, with perhaps 48 hours left, and Bordo was due to fly out very early the next day. She had been on the road for 12 straight days and had a Reiki appointment booked for 3:30 that afternoon.

She had woken at 4 a.m. with the old instinct: to get on a plane immediately. “Let me just hold that impulse,” she told herself, weighing it against the appointment. “Am I a fraud to my own book?”

Arriving with nothing left to give her friend, she reasoned, wouldn’t help either of them, and she knew what the next five days would demand. She kept the appointment.

The well-worn path of the people pleaser is still there, even for someone who wrote a book about questioning it. At 4 a.m., it was waiting.

“I think we’re all questioning all the time,” she told me. “This is still new. I was a people pleaser for far longer than I have been sovereign.”

The well-worn path of the people pleaser is still there, even for someone who wrote a book about questioning it. At 4 a.m., it was waiting. But we all know that if you do what you always did, you get what you always got.

That doesn’t quiet the voice insisting you should be doing more. When I asked about the harsh inner critic, Bordo tied it to fear and to something she calls “a permission of worth.”

“I feel like if you believe that you are allowed a life that is true and well and free, then that sets the table for a different list. That will yield that list that you are talking about. The list moves. The list changes.”

I know how to manage my disease. Watching the plan fall apart yet again, and then living with the aftermath, is what wears me down.

I know that list well. I was 14 when I was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease. In 2007, in my early 30s, after medical complications, I had my intestine removed, and hoped the hardest part was behind me. Instead came hernias, mesh infections, and more surgery, with complications continuing for years before things finally settled in early 2025.

I assumed my 50s would be easier. Then I got shingles, and with an immune system like mine, an ordinary illness set off six months of fallout. At 51 came a cancer scare unrelated to my autoimmune disease, followed by more surgery and recovery. My body has to recalibrate every time. Each setback is one more timeout, one more delay.

I know how to manage my disease. Watching the plan fall apart yet again, and then living with the aftermath, is what wears me down. It’s a particular kind of fatigue, the kind that comes from having it all on repeat, and underneath it there’s resentment, and sometimes anger. I feel overwhelmed, and quite often defeated, and a voice tells me I should be handling all of it better.

Wanting things to be different is like writing the check for more suffering. Some days I need a leg up, or just a break. When I catch myself in that loop, I know I still have work to do.

This is where I wanted to press, because the territory is slippery. You can notice that you tend to neglect yourself without concluding that the neglect made you sick. Bordo is firm on this.

“We didn’t do anything to deserve what’s happened to us,” she says. “Not ever.”

“We didn’t do anything to deserve what’s happened to us,” she says. “Not ever.”

She also acknowledges the limits of her perspective: “I’m not a doctor and you know that,” emphasizing that she’s speaking from personal experience rather than offering a medical explanation.

Looking back, she sees a pattern of ignoring symptoms because they showed up at inconvenient times, while she kept putting coworkers, family, and friends first. She had watched women exhaust themselves for other people’s needs, and it looked normal to her.

Then the diagnoses arrived. She described the experience of suddenly having to confront her own needs after spending so much of her life focused on everyone else’s.

“That is when the human being actually needs to come online the loudest, not the human doing,” she says.

“I had a disease in my body. I had cancer in my body. I had toxicity in my body.” For a while, it felt too big to tackle. “Self-forgiveness came first,” she says, though she knew she hadn’t caused or earned any of it.

We hear a lot about forgiveness being a gift you give yourself. We hear less about the self-flagellation that can accompany illness and other difficult experiences, particularly when we find ourselves wondering whether we could have done something differently.

Self-forgiveness can be difficult, especially when we’re accustomed to extending more understanding to others than to ourselves. I recognize that tendency in my own life, too, and I understand why Bordo chose to begin there.

“There wasn’t really a Sara,” she recalls. She had spent her life working out who she needed to be to stay “liked, loved, and safe.” She also realized how much authority she’d handed to other people over her own well-being. That pattern, she told me, “boils over from personal to professional to medical.”

These days, Bordo says she’s learning to give greater weight to her own experiences and needs, rather than relying solely on external measures of how she’s doing. For her, this means recognizing the value of her own perspective alongside medical information, rather than treating the two as mutually exclusive.

“Those choices and framework had to be rewritten and re-authored by me,” she says. That work, she added, began when she reached a particularly difficult point in her life.

Recognizing a pattern doesn’t necessarily mean we can immediately break it, particularly when illness, relationships, and circumstances influence the choices available to us.

I told her I believe agency and accountability are part of this too, and I know the word “permission” can be complicated for some readers. She doesn’t pretend it won’t be.

Bordo knew her book wouldn’t resonate with everyone. Some readers find her approach too focused on the mind-body connection, while others interpret her emphasis on personal agency as suggesting that people who struggle to make changes are somehow choosing to remain stuck. She recognizes that her message may be received differently than she intends.

Our conversation left me thinking about how complicated change can be. Recognizing a pattern doesn’t necessarily mean we can immediately break it, particularly when illness, relationships, and circumstances influence the choices available to us.

I do know what she says to the people who keep going in circles: “I want more for you.”

#9247. Designing With Uncertainty: How AI Supercharges Probabilistic Thinking

Pratik Joglekar is a Senior Product Designer working with HubSpot. He loves to solve complex and challenging UX problems. When not working, he can be found at … More about Pratik ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In 2024, an Air Canada customer asked a chatbot about bereavement fares. The bot confidently gave him a refund policy that didn’t exist. The airline refused to honor it. A tribunal ruled in the customer’s favor. The bot hadn’t decided anything; it had predicted an answer based on patterns in its training data. The company treated that prediction as policy.

This is the risk at the heart of designing with AI today: probabilistic systems wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The AI offers a guess, the interface presents it as truth, and the user, or the organization, acts on it.

Humans are wired for deterministic thinking. We prefer to believe that past actions determine future outcomes. Flip a coin 999 times and get heads every time, the deterministic mind assumes the coin is rigged. The probabilistic mind accepts that the 1000th flip could still go either way. That second mindset is harder to hold onto, but it is exactly what designers need right now.

Products operate in complex, nonlinear environments, and AI is accelerating that complexity. When designers and product teams treat AI outputs as the answer rather than one of many possible answers, they build fragile experiences, and in some cases, like medical diagnostics or financial forecasting, genuinely dangerous ones.

This article is a practical guide to designing probabilistically with AI as a partner. It is about using AI to sharpen your thinking rather than outsource it, accounting for model bias, human sentiment, and perceived risk along the way.

Most questions we ask AI do not produce binary answers. They produce probabilities based on patterns in data. If you ask, “Do aliens exist?” the answer will be somewhere between plausible and uncertain. Scientists consider life elsewhere in the universe likely, but without any concrete evidence, we cannot confirm it. The answer doesn’t resolve the question; it frames it as a probability.

Designers should read AI outputs the same way. They are signals, not conclusions, possible outcomes that have to be interpreted within the context of product goals, user behavior, and business constraints.

Many digital products already work this way. Netflix doesn’t know you’ll enjoy Superstore because you watched The Office; it estimates the probability and surfaces the title accordingly. The interface is responding to a prediction.

Design decisions can follow the same logic. AI models can combine behavioral analytics with research insights to estimate the likelihood of certain outcomes, and those probabilities can act as a yardstick for design strategy. Consider a scenario where analytics suggest a 60% versus 90% confidence that users will complete a purchase. At 60%, the design has to do more persuasive work, testimonials, explanations, comparisons, and reassurance signals may help the user move toward a decision. At 90%, the user is already motivated, and the design should start removing friction so the action can happen quickly. Same screen, very different design problem.

AI can also simulate outcomes using historical data and behavioral models before you commit to a direction. The value of those simulations depends heavily on how prompts are structured, the context they define, the hypothesis being tested, user motivation, and the edge cases you want stressed.

I can think of one such practical use: evaluating early designs through structured prompts, especially when you don’t have direct access to the user group you’re designing for. The prompt below is a starting point for evaluating a design from the perspective of neurodivergent users as well. Treat it as a template, adapt the user group, criteria, and output format to your product, and use it as a conversation starter with your team rather than a verdict.

That said, simulations do not replace experimentation. Because models are trained on historical data, they reflect past behavior more strongly than they predict future change. Imagine designing a voice interface for elderly users who struggle with touchscreens. A model trained on mobile interaction data might predict low engagement, not because the idea lacks value, but because the dataset reflects different user behavior. Simulations should always surface assumptions, not prevent innovation.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

AI systems are built on historical data, more specifically, on the datasets they are trained on. That foundation shapes the outputs we receive. During the AI Summit in France, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi shared an example that illustrates this well. If you ask an AI model to generate an image of a person writing with the left hand, the output may still show a person writing with their right hand. The reason is statistical: most people are right-handed, and the training data reflects that. This may have improved over time, but the point remains relevant. I still occasionally see this behavior when generating images with similar models.

What you receive is not truth. It is the most statistically likely outcome given the data available. Always ask whether past data meaningfully predicts future behavior. If additional context can improve the prediction, include it. Without context, the output is just one of many possible answers dressed up as the only one.

Confidence scores deserve the same scrutiny. Overtrusting a high-confidence output leads to the Air Canada situation. Dismissing a low-confidence one can cause teams to miss a real signal buried in noisy data. A prediction with 90% confidence is not necessarily correct, and a 40% signal is not necessarily useless. Designers must still weigh the possibilities, consider the case in front of them, and bring judgment to what the AI recommends.

Transparency is how you make that possible. As AI systems increasingly shape decisions, people need visibility into how outputs are generated, the sources, the reasoning, and the summaries behind a recommendation. Black-box systems breed distrust. Systems that reveal their reasoning let users evaluate outputs for themselves. That transparency is good design and ethical practice. It respects the trust people place in these tools.

Thinking in probabilities often means resisting the temptation of quick answers. AI can accelerate research and surface patterns faster than ever before, but those outputs are starting points, not final decisions.

Design shapes how a product is ultimately experienced — the decisions designers make determine whether the experience feels adequate, intuitive, or exceptional. And design is inherently full of assumptions and bets. Even the most rigorous research can yield multiple valid solutions to the same problem, each carrying a different probability of success.

Thinking probabilistically means recognizing that design decisions rarely produce binary outcomes. They lead to a range of possible results, and the role of the designer is to navigate those possibilities and identify the path most likely to create value. This mindset also builds adaptability: user needs evolve, strategies change, and sometimes ideas fail. Teams that lean on data signals, experimentation, and learning loops move faster toward the most effective solution.

Before the practical principles, one fundamental idea:

Design decisions should be optimized for likelihood, not certainty.

Every design decision is a bet, not a guarantee. Even when decisions are informed by research and data, they are still based on smaller samples and assumptions about how users will behave at scale. A well-researched idea can still fail in the real world.

The Air Canada chatbot from the introduction is a design lesson as much as a legal one. The bot was doing what language models do, predicting plausible text. The interface, however, communicated that prediction with complete confidence, no caveats, no “here’s what our policy usually says,” no obvious path to a human. The user read confidence as commitment, and legally, so did the tribunal.

This is what happens when probabilistic systems are wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The interface transforms likelihood into certainty, and that is where the risk emerges.

Designers should avoid binary thinking — a great idea does not mean guaranteed success, and a familiar idea is not guaranteed to fail. Examine variations, confidence levels, and edge cases instead. AI can certainly help here, acting as a portfolio-thinking engine that surfaces different interpretations, highlights risks, and generates structured recommendations. The goal is not to optimize for certainty, but for value: it should always be value-driven.

Think of the moment in Avengers: Infinity War when Doctor Strange tells Tony Stark that out of millions of possible futures, there is only one where they win. AI cannot tell you the future, but it can help you explore the possible paths. Instead of asking whether an idea will succeed, ask AI to estimate the likelihood and get a score, and use those signals to guide decisions.

Even an actual probability is not a final answer. Imagine an AI model predicts an 80% likelihood that users prefer a minimal checkout experience. That does not mean the solution is simply “build a minimal checkout.” Data should function as a compass, not a map.

These questions help designers validate predictions through usability testing and additional research. AI excels at identifying patterns, but it rarely explains why those patterns exist. Understanding motivation is still a human-centered research task.

The clearest cautionary tale here is Amazon’s experimental AI recruitment tool, which the company reportedly scrapped after discovering that the model had learned to downgrade resumes from women. The training data, roughly a decade of historical hiring decisions, was skewed toward male candidates, and the model inherited that skew. It began penalizing resumes that included the word “women’s,” as in “women’s chess club captain,” and favoring language more commonly found on men’s resumes. The system was not intentionally biased — the data was. Amazon reportedly tried to adjust it and eventually shut the project down because they could not guarantee it would not surface other discriminatory patterns.

Examples like this are why interpreting AI output critically matters. Designers need to understand the data behind a prediction and evaluate the reliability of the models they depend on. A recommendation is only as good as the data it was trained on, and the only way to know what that data is hiding is to ask.

Experimentation is usually framed as a way to validate a design decision. Want to lift the click-through rate of a CTA? Run an A/B test. Probabilistic thinking reframes this. Experiments should not only confirm solutions but also reduce uncertainty.

Traditional A/B testing is expensive. It costs engineering time, traffic allocation, and user exposure, especially when a losing variant runs against a significant chunk of your audience. AI simulations can help filter weaker ideas before they reach production by making experimentation more efficient. User needs shift constantly, and the most effective teams iterate fast.

AI can help evaluate assumptions early by modeling potential outcomes based on historical and behavioral data. These simulations act as a hypothesis filter, pointing to the directions worth investing engineering effort in. This also supports personalization — different users may respond better to different experiences. Version A may resonate with high-intent users while version B works better for exploratory ones. Multiple experiences living side by side are not a flaw; they can be an intentional strategy.

AI amplifies probabilistic thinking by surfacing scenarios, assigning likelihood scores, and enabling personalization at scale. Experimentation becomes a continuous feedback loop:

Predict → Test → Learn → Adjust → Repeat!

Use this template to define the hypothesis:

We believe [behavioral assumption] will impact [metric] because [reason]. We’ll know we are right when [evidence].

Example: We believe simplifying the onboarding flow from 5 steps to 3 will increase completion rate because users experience decision fatigue when too many choices are presented. We’ll know we’re right when we see at least a 15% increase in step-to-step conversion with no drop in activation rate.

One of the hardest things for designers is making uncertainty understandable and actionable. When uncertainty is hidden, users treat AI outputs as facts. When it’s communicated clearly, trust increases.

Ranges, estimates, and confidence indicators go a long way. A delivery window of “Friday to Monday” tells the truth about variability without misleading anyone, whereas a specific timestamp that slips erodes trust every time. A face recognition feature that says “this looks like Pratik, is that right?” sets more honest expectations than one that just labels the photo with a name.

Communicating uncertainty does not weaken trust — it strengthens it. The goal is not to eliminate uncertainty but to design for it intelligently.

Different users respond to uncertainty differently, and your design should account for that:

AI should augment human judgment, and certainly not replace it. The most trustworthy systems are designed with clear moments where people can review, challenge, correct, or override machine suggestions. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is not a safety net — it is a refinement engine. Every override, correction, or rejection becomes high-quality feedback that improves the model over time.

Control is a prerequisite for adoption. Users are more willing to rely on AI when they understand how a suggestion was generated, can evaluate its implications, and can easily intervene. Well-designed products make this explicit: who is acting, what happens if the suggestion is wrong, and where the user can step in.

These interactions are also critical for system improvement. Every accept, reject, or edit is a strong signal, and compared to passive analytics, this kind of feedback produces far more meaningful training data. It closes the loop between real-world usage and model performance.

GitHub Copilot is a good everyday example. It offers inline code suggestions that developers can accept with a tab, edit, or ignore entirely. The system never commits code on the user’s behalf. Authorship stays with the humans. Every data point becomes implicit feedback about which suggestions were useful. Gmail’s Smart Compose works similarly, presenting predicted text as optional, keeping tone and intent in the user’s hands.

In higher-stakes contexts, HITL becomes more explicit. Risk and fraud systems typically use probability scores to route decisions: low-risk: proceed automatically; medium-risk: trigger additional verification; and high-risk: escalate to a human reviewer. This balances speed with judgment without removing oversight.

In safety-critical domains like healthcare, human oversight is non-negotiable. AI may flag anomalies or suggest a diagnosis, but the clinician retains final authority. Tools that explain the details help the practitioner understand why a recommendation was made, reinforcing confidence without removing accountability.

From a UX perspective, HITL is about matching the interaction pattern to the level of risk. Simple accept/reject affordances work well for low-risk suggestions that improve speed without real consequences. As the stakes climb, impacting data, money, or people, preview and approval steps become essential. Explanations help users calibrate trust rather than blindly accept outputs.

What happens behind the scenes matters just as much. The system should capture user decisions with context, feed them into learning workflows, and log overrides for auditability. Over time, teams can track signals like override rate, confidence accuracy, time-to-approval, and perceived trust. A high override rate is not a user failure. It is a signal that the design or the model needs attention.

Poorly implemented HITL systems can fail in subtle ways. Human review can devolve into a rubber stamp. Workflows can slow down so much that users route around the safeguards. Feedback can skew toward a narrow subset of users. These risks are real, but they are design problems, not reasons to remove HITL.

The goal is not to maximize human involvement. It is to focus it where uncertainty, impact, or ethics demand it. Keeping HITL is less about control and more about clarity: clarity about who decides, when uncertainty matters, and how responsibility is shared between people and machines.

Good design adapts as the landscape shifts. Product design, especially in AI-powered systems, can no longer afford to optimize only for short-term conversion metrics. User intent is fluid as well as ever-changing, environments change rapidly, and probabilistic systems continuously evolve too. What works today can quietly break tomorrow. Designing for resilience means building products that stay reliable, trustworthy, and useful even as assumptions, data, and user behaviors change.

Resilient design shifts the question from:

How do we maximize this metric right now?! → How does this system behave over time, under stress, and in uncertainty?

Do not just consider last quarter’s numbers. Peek into the following quarters to identify the shift and make changes accordingly.

Likelihoods shift constantly, AI models drift, contexts evolve, and user needs mature as well, so designing as if conditions are stable creates fragility in probabilistic environments. A resilient approach assumes volatility as the default.

Think about how recommendation systems tend to evolve. The early version of a content feed optimizes for engagement, and for a while, engagement goes up. Then users start to notice the feed feels narrow, repetitive, maybe even exhausting. Resilient systems rebalance, introducing novelty, diversifying signals, and pulling in long-term satisfaction measures alongside short-term clicks.

Short-term conversion gains often hide long-term costs. Speeding up onboarding can reduce comprehension. Maximizing notification CTR can erode trust. Optimizing engagement alone can produce unhealthy usage patterns. Fragile systems maximize numbers while ignoring second-order effects, the downstream consequences that show up weeks or months later.

Duolingo’s hearts system is a good example of designing against this. It introduces friction: if you make too many mistakes, you run out of hearts and have to wait or practice older material to earn more. On paper, that looks like a conversion killer: fewer lessons per session. In practice, the team has publicly discussed how it supports long-term motivation and retention, which is the metric that actually matters for a learning app. Short-term engagement dips, but long-term outcomes improve.

Meta has made a similar, if more reluctant, shift. The company publicly acknowledged that optimizing purely for “time spent” produced unintended emotional and societal effects, which led to a stated pivot toward “meaningful social interactions” as a guiding metric. Whether that shift fully landed is up for debate, but the acknowledgment itself is the point: optimizing for the wrong thing at scale has real downstream cost.

Teams routinely plan for traffic spikes, but rarely for uncertainty spikes. Yet AI systems degrade, adversarial behaviors evolve, and external shocks can reshape user behavior overnight. Resilient design assumes variability and prepares for it.

This means designing for degrading confidence. What does your interface do when the AI isn’t sure? Does it quietly fail, or does it gracefully hand off? Does the experience still make sense if AI assistance goes away entirely? A good fallback strategy is as important as the happy path.

If you take one thing from this article into your next design review, make it this:

That single reframe changes how you write hypotheses, interpret AI output, scope experiments, and design for the moments when the system is wrong. Starting this week, name the assumption behind every AI recommendation you accept, find one place in your product where a probabilistic output is presented as a certainty, fix the framing, and design the fallback before the happy path.

The shift from deterministic to probabilistic design is less about new tools and more about a new posture. AI has not introduced uncertainty into our world. It has simply made the uncertainty that was always there impossible to ignore. AI can estimate, simulate, and recommend, but it cannot decide what matters, which users are being overlooked, or which unconventional idea is worth defending against a model trained on yesterday’s data. Those remain human responsibilities. Think in ranges, not points. Test assumptions, not features. Build for adaptation, not perfection. In a world where prediction is cheap, and judgment is rare, the most valuable thing a designer can do is keep asking, What else might be true?

#9246. Snapshots Of Summer (July 2026 Wallpapers Edition)

Cosima has been an editor at SmashingMag since 2013. Whenever she’s not writing articles for the weekly Smashing Newsletter, she’s probably working on a … More about Cosima ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The scent of rain after a hot day, watching the moon rise on a summer night’s sky, or going for a swim in a nearby lake — July is full of small, distinctive moments that can quietly spark new inspiration. So, why not bring a bit of that summer joy to your desktop, too, this month?

For this post, artists and designers from across the globe once again tickled their creativity and designed desktop wallpapers that capture that very special July feeling, just as it has been a monthly tradition here at Smashing Magazine for more than 15 years already. You’ll find their creations compiled below, along with a selection of summery favorites from our wallpapers archives that are just too good to be forgotten.

A huge thank-you to everyone who shared their designs with us this month — this post wouldn’t be possible without your wonderful support! If you too would like to get featured in one of our upcoming wallpapers posts, please don’t hesitate to join in. We can’t wait to see your story come to life! Happy July!

“There is a quiet, hypnotic rhythm that exists just beneath the surface of our busy lives. When we slow down enough to notice, we see that the universe moves in beautiful, repeating circles — in the way light filters through water, how leaves dance as they fall, and how we are drawn together in moments of shared peace. True balance isn't about standing perfectly still; it is a fluid, continuous motion.” — Designed by PopArt Studio from Novi Sad, Serbia.

“Vincent van Gogh’s sunflowers are among my favorite paintings, and I’ve designed a papercraft version loosely inspired by them. A perfect theme for the beginning of summer.” — Designed by Caroline Boire from France.

“We hope July turns out to be a wonderful month, one that stays with us so vividly that we find ourselves wanting to ‘go back to the future’ time and again. Wishing you a month full of enjoyment and rest!” — Designed by Veronica Valenzuela from Spain.

“July 7 is World Chocolate Day. A perfectly reasonable excuse for a strawberry to spend the afternoon floating in chocolate.” — Designed by Ginger IT Solutions from Serbia.

“Where soft skies meet endless green, peace finds it’s place.” — Designed by Swati Gohil from India.

“I created this wallpaper as a daily visual push to stay focused, take risks, and turn dreams into reality.” — Designed by Hitesh Puri from Delhi, India.

Once a week. Useful tips on front-end & UX. Trusted by 207.000 friendly folks.

“Moments of July marked in sunlight, sea breeze, and sky — a quiet snapshot of summer, worn at the edges like a well-traveled postcard.” — Designed by Libra Fire from Serbia.

Designed by Xenia Latii from Berlin, Germany.

“July in South Africa is dreary and wintery so we give all the southern hemisphere dwellers a bit of color for those gray days. And for the northern hemisphere dwellers a bit of pop for their summer!” — Designed by Wonderland Collective from South Africa.

Designed by Lieke Dol from the Netherlands.

“July is the middle of summer, when most of us go on road trips, so I designed a calendar inspired by my love of traveling and summer holidays.” — Designed by Patricia Coroi from Romania.

“In times of clean eating and the world of superfoods there is one vegetable missing. An old, forgotten one. A flower actually. Rare and special. Once it had a royal reputation (I cheated a bit with the blue). The artichocke — this is my superhero in the garden! I am a food lover — you too? Enjoy it, dip it!” — Designed by Alexandra Tamgnoué from Germany.

“Make sure you have a refreshing source of ideas, plans, and hopes this July. Especially if you are to escape from urban life for a while.” — Designed by Igor Izhik from Canada.

“Ever watched Joe’s Apartment when you were a kid? Well, that movie left a soft spot in my heart for the little critters. Don’t get me wrong: I won’t invite them over for dinner, but I won’t grab my flip flop and bring the wrath upon them when I see one running in the house. So there you have it… three roaches… bringing the smack down on that pesky human… ZZZZZZZAP!!” — Designed by Wonderland Collective from South Africa.

#9245. Psychedelics: Are We Repeating Timothy Leary’s Mistakes?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Today's psychedelic renaissance traces back to Timothy Leary, the colorful Harvard psychologist whose slogan, “Turn on, tune in, drop out,” became a prescription for the counterculture.

Today, in an era of ubiquitous artificial intelligence (AI) and brain studies, looking to the 1960s for answers seems almost quaint. But history has its uses, especially if we seem determined to repeat it.

Professors Leary and Alpert led the Harvard Psilocybin Project, highlighting potential therapeutic and mystical applications of psychedelics like psilocybin for treating addiction, anxiety, and depression.

But advocacy increasingly overshadowed research. Leary's Concord Prison Experiment suggested psilocybin reduced criminal recidivism. Later evaluations—like a 34-year follow-up of the Concord Prison Experiment—found claims of lasting treatment effects were erroneous.

By 1963, Harvard dismissed Leary. He was obsessed with personal intoxication and circumventing both student safeguards and academic caution. His counterculture advocacy helped trigger a strong cultural backlash and subsequent psychedelic criminalization.

Today’s psychedelic trials avoid Leary’s mistakes by emphasizing strict screening, clinical oversight, and controlled settings.

And modern psychiatry has great hopes for psychedelics. Yet psychedelic trials face distinctive challenges. For example, patients know when they receive the active drug, and their expectations influence outcomes. Therapists also may be true believers.

Meanwhile, the RAND Psychedelics Survey estimates that roughly 11 million American adults used psilocybin in the past year. But support is greatest for FDA approval. Approval for psilocybin among military veterans was only 24% for general legal use but 54% for FDA-approved therapy. Yet passing legislation, opening psychedelic centers, and obtaining FDA approval are very different accomplishments.

Oregon voters approved the measure, and psilocybin centers opened in 2023. Adults 21 years and older (including out-of-state visitors) may access services with no medical diagnosis, prescription, or referral.

Unlike a retail cannabis dispensary, clients can’t buy takeout mushrooms. Instead, services require a mandatory preparation session, on-site administration of up to 50 mg of psilocybin under the supervision of a state-licensed facilitator, and an optional follow-up integration session.

An August 2026 JAMA Network Open study of 346 participants at 24 licensed centers by P. Todd Korthuis, MD, and colleagues offers a landmark real-world dataset and cautionary tale for policymakers.

Participants described improvements in depression, anxiety, PTSD symptoms, well-being, and life satisfaction. But there was no control group, randomization, or representative patient population.

Also, 4 participants (1.2%), psychedelic novices, experienced serious behavioral adverse reactions requiring emergency care.

However, 3 of the 4 participants who experienced serious adverse reactions nevertheless described their experience as highly meaningful.

Meaningful? Certainly. Therapeutic? Not necessarily.

A separate WUSTL mystery-shopper study found that centers took screening seriously. I previously reviewed this study in detail.

Although legally framed around general personal growth and wellness, Oregon data show the vast majority of clients seek services for specific mental health struggles. According to the OPS 2025 Year in Review, the top reported reasons for seeking psilocybin were anxiety, depression, PTSD, and other trauma.

Three months from treatment, 4.5% of participants reported persistent/worsening depression, 1.9% reported thoughts of death or suicide, and 8.7% reported symptoms suggesting possible hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder (HPPD).

A recent NPR report highlighted severe, lingering psychological destabilization in some patients following psychedelic clinical trials. Yet post-psychedelic risks, ranging from panic attacks to suicidal ideation and dissociation, are frequently overlooked.

Psychiatrist and neuroscientist David Rabin wrote in the Los Angeles Times that roughly half his clinical time is spent helping patients recover from challenging drug experiences. Some patients are frightened or disconnected. Others believe they discovered universal truths. As Rabin put it, “Certainty is a hell of a drug.”

Patients may suffer from persistent anxiety, perceptual disturbances, psychiatric deterioration, or destabilization of their understanding of themselves and reality. Prior screening before taking psychedelics cannot accurately identify everyone at risk.

In addiction medicine, we learned long ago that successful detoxification isn’t the same as recovery from addiction. Similarly, completing a psychedelic session and not experiencing an emergency isn’t itself evidence of long-term safety.

Two new neuroscience studies deserve attention.

Gudmundsen and colleagues, reporting in Nature Communications, found distinct metabolic effects of psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B in rats, with modest, drug-dependent changes detectable one week later. Only some changes were shared across all three drugs. A healthy person who takes 2C-B and one who takes psilocybin don’t run the same risks.

In Science Advances, Delgado-Sallent and colleagues in BU's Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences reported that psilocybin and ketamine altered decision-making strategies and orbitofrontal activity in mice. At selected doses, decisions became slower but more accurate, suggesting that psychedelics change brain-wide configurations and local dynamics to promote more deliberate, flexible, and sensory-driven decisions.

Neither study establishes human brain injury, and neither shows lasting clinical benefits. But there are known and unknown risks with psychedelics. Treating severe illness justifies accepting some risk and uncertainty.

Psychedelics appear to change the brain. But who needs their brain changed?

Opening a window for change doesn't determine what’s actually learned in the experience. In a clinical setting, therapy shapes that window. At a party, a retreat, or with a charismatic guide, something else may climb through that window of opportunity; for example, psychedelics may unmask psychosis or mania in someone who looked and felt fine.

Insights may feel valid without being true.

Psychedelics increase emotional openness, suggestibility, and trust. These characteristics may facilitate therapy. Alternatively, sometimes they facilitate exploitation.

Undue influence and misconduct are potential problems. People in a highly suggestible state are easier to exploit.

A 2024 JAMA Network Open consensus statement led by Amy McGuire addressed informed consent, physical touch, professional boundaries, training, and accountability.

Consent to take a psychedelic is not a blank check, as far as consent is concerned.

Physical touch is ethically fraught in conventional psychotherapy. Add psychedelic intoxication, disorientation, heightened suggestibility, and a patient asking to be held—what could possibly go wrong?

Patients need explicit boundaries. They also need the ongoing ability to withdraw consent, and independent channels to report misconduct

The therapist’s good intentions are not a safeguarding protocol.

When I began studying addiction, it was considered a moral failure.

Changing neurotransmission is relatively easy. Producing sustained recovery is considerably harder.

Neuroplasticity is an opportunity, not a clinical outcome. Addiction itself demonstrates that experience-dependent brain plasticity is not invariably beneficial.

Consequently, so far, claims that one psychedelic session can replace years of psychotherapy exceed available evidence.

Six decades ago, Leary popularized psychedelic experiences before demonstrating therapeutic value. Today we know better.

The psychedelic trip ends. The biological and psychological consequences may not. Also, if a subsequent issue arises, who responds? Who provides treatment? Who pays? This seems unclear.

Treatment-resistant depression, trauma, PTSD, GAD, and addiction warrant innovative treatments. In contrast, existential uncertainty isn’t a condition requiring pharmacological intervention.

Turn on the science. Tune out the hype. And don't drop the patient.

#9244. Exhibition celebrates Delftware, the Dutch art form that became the ‘Ikea of its day’

Ceramics in Blue Loves You, “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever” Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag

On a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark new Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people. “There was no one there because ceramics can feel cold and distanced,” she says. “They can be hard to bring alive, because the makers are anonymous, and [the objects are] often displayed in glass cases.”

But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different. The result, Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, opens this month at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague, where she is the curator of decorative arts. It will, she says, be “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever”. Equally importantly, she promises it will be captivating and enjoyable.

“Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she says. “We want to show the love craftspeople put into these pieces. It has inspired, and it continues to inspire, so many craftmakers—we’ll give them a platform.”

Natasja Sadi's Suikerbloemen (2024) Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag, photo: Studio Roodenburch

Around 1,000 objects, including vases, teapots, plates, wall plaques and tiles, will be on display at the Kunstmuseum, which has one of the largest collections of the art form that is perhaps the best-known cultural export of the Netherlands. Also on show in Blue Loves You will be Delftware-inspired pieces, including the blue dress worn by Queen Máxima of the Netherlands for her husband’s 2013 investiture, its bodice embroidered with Delft-derived flowers. “There’s a lot more to it than blue and white fridge magnets,” Lambooy says.

Although the porcelain is known for its characteristic colouring, the show will include examples of both white and multicoloured Delftware. It will explore its history, dating back to the 17th century. The form was originally a high-end Chinese import, displayed in the wealthiest homes. But when factories started to make their own version of it in Delft, it was transformed.

“It became an on-trend, functional brand that was affordable for every home and on every budget: it was the Ikea of its day,” says Lambooy, whose co-curator for the long-term show is the television presenter Janny van der Heijden (who is also a judge on the country’s version of The Great British Bake Off).

Ceramics in Blue Loves You, “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever” Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag

The quintessential Delftware piece was the tulip pyramid, some of the best examples of which were made for King William III, born in The Hague, and his English wife Queen Mary II, who were the joint monarchs of England, Scotland and Ireland in the late 17th century. “Mary exported Delftware to Britain—she was the most important woman in its history,” Lambooy says.

The porcelain’s connections to Dutch colonialism will also be explored, with exhibits including an installation of sugar flowers by the floral artist Natasja Sadi, whose family are originally from the former Dutch colony of Suriname and whose ancestors were enslaved.

• Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, Kunstmuseum, The Hague, 28 November-31 December 2029

#9243. Bát Tràng Museum

Designed by M — N Associates, Ho Chi Minh City

The Bát Tràng Museum stands as the first private museum authorized by the government within Bát Tràng Village, founded by National Artist Vũ Đức Thắng. Originally named “Hồn Đất Việt” — translated as “Viet’s Ceramic Soul” — this museum embodies his remarkable legacy. Vũ Đức Thắng gained widespread recognition for his spectacular creation of 12 remarkably genuine pottery boots, earning the Guinness Record in 2013. His artistic skills include a collection of modern artworks highlighted by two unique techniques: color-changing ceramic glaze and intricate three-dimensional sculpting. These methods display his mastery and creativity in ceramic art.

We carefully researched and studied to include his unique artistic techniques and style in creating a new look for the museum. This involved giving the museum a new name and creating a unique custom typeface MN Vũ Thắng with “pottery-shoes-soul” inktrap touches. We wanted to echo his process and masterpieces into the content system.

The brand’s visual system was created to resonate with the beauty of the various unique artworks while systematizing them into an archive through a new, clean photography style. A deliberate pottery silhouette canvas was employed for buttons and patterns across different applications, maintaining a unique and relative aesthetic. This design approach bonded to a grid system inspired by the 3-parts floor plan layout of the museum, ensuring consistency and structure throughout the brand’s visual elements.

We simplified the color palette, emphasizing the vividness and authenticity of the artwork, especially the rich colors and textures of the ceramic glaze. This focused approach highlights the authentic essence of each piece, elevating their visual impact while preserving their nature.

Collaboratively, we aimed to assemble the Bát Tràng Museum towards a more contemporary style while preserving its rich heritage.

#9242. Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

Mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast. He’s spent years building everything from crypto … More about Mikhail ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

We know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a

with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working.

That gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable.

Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem.

For years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into.

Audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR, you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well.

But audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple new features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way.

The WebAIM Million report, which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and ‘vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds.

Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose.

With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies.

Start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you “fully give in to the vibes” and “forget that the code even exists”. You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated.

Models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And

#9241. Capitalism and the Millennial Midlife Crisis

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Many studies have shown that the shape of happiness over time is ironically smile-shaped—gradually decreasing until reaching an all-time low at midlife before rebounding. And like the good little consumers we are, we try to spend our way out of the drop. We try to fill the void with shiny things instead of doing the deep inner work needed for self-actualization,

Big purchases have always been a landmark of the midlife crisis. Luxury cars, vacation properties, and other extravagant, ill-advised symbols of the good life are subconsciously used to soothe midpoint ennui. While millennials aren’t immune to this, our relationship with capitalism is more of a complicated situationship than marital bliss, and that changes things.

Millennials are characterized as the first generation who are worse off than their parents. As usual, this headline isn’t the whole picture. What has changed is the spread of wealth. The wealth gap is vast and increasing. So, while some millennials are off buying the classic toys of the midlife crisis, others are struggling to make ends meet, and there is little in between. For struggling millennials, affordability and housing crises have intersected with midlife. So how are most millennials shopping at life’s midpoint?

Even if your needs are met, midlife can sometimes mean wishing for something more, better, or different, and there is nothing wrong with that. In fact, it’s quite normal! So, as you decide the choose your own adventure of the modern midlife crisis, here are some questions you might ask yourself:

Not all midlife-fueled spending is created equal. Some purchases may feel good in the moment but draw you further from your ideal life. And your ideal life may be very different from your peers’ or your parents’. Comparison is the thief of joy; try to avoid it. And if you can’t, at least compare apples to apples. The home you can afford may look much different than the one you grew up in, but it was harder for you to purchase because of factors outside your control. Contextualize and celebrate your achievements.

My midlife splurge has involved buying a rustic off-grid cabin with my friends. Splitting the modest purchase four ways has made it more affordable and more exciting. It’s an investment in the type of future I want: one that centers tranquility and close relationships. I love these people and being away from the chaos of the modern age. This cabin is a symbol of my commitment to them and the sort of life we want to build together. I won’t be drawn in by the mirage of a generic good life. I will decide what fulfillment means to me. I hope you do too.

1. University of Cambridge. (2023, November 16). Millennials aren’t all worse off than baby boomers, but the rich-poor gap is widening. ScienceDaily. https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/11/231113111750.htm
